usage: 전부 paired with 다 doubles the emphasis
전부 here works as an adverb 'completely'
examples: 과자를 전부 줄게.
I'll give you all the snacks.
Casual 반말; 전부 as the object 'the whole lot'
손님이 전부 떠났어요.
All the guests left.
전부 covers every single person in the group
서류를 전부 확인했는지 다시 점검하겠습니다.
I'll double-check whether all the documents have been reviewed.
Formal workplace register; 전부 = the entire set, nothing skipped
nuance: 전부 is the Sino-Korean noun 全部 ('whole' 全 + 'part' 部, literally 'the whole of every part'), meaning the complete quantity with absolutely nothing left out. The nearest rival is the native word 다: 다 is a pure adverb ('all' / 'completely') and never takes a particle, while 전부 is a noun that can be a subject (전부가), an object (전부를), or stand adverbially — and the two are so close that Koreans habitually stack them as 전부 다 for extra force. Watch the dividing line with 모두: 모두 leans toward 'everyone, every person' and is a touch more formal, whereas 전부 leans toward 'the whole amount/thing'. 전부 is neutral and works in both casual speech and formal writing. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the English 'all the' that glues onto a noun: you don't say 전부 책 — you say 책 전부 or 모든 책, because 전부 follows the noun (or stands alone) rather than premodifying it like 모든.

mistakes: Writing 전부 책 ('all books') by copying English 'all the books': 전부 cannot premodify like English 'all'. Use 책 전부 ('the books, all of them') or 모든 책.
Using 전부 when you mean 대부분 ('most'). 전부 leaves out nothing; if a few are excluded, you must say 대부분.
Forcing a particle where 전부 is acting as an adverb, e.g. 전부를 먹었어요 when you just mean 'I ate it all' — 전부 다 먹었어요 is the natural choice.

usage: 절반 = exactly one of two equal parts
절반 attached to a whole via possessive 의
examples: 사탕을 절반 나눠 줄게.
I'll split the candy in half for you.
Casual; 절반 as the shared portion
학생의 절반이 시험에 합격했어요.
Half of the students passed the exam.
절반이 = half of a group as subject
예산의 절반 이상이 인건비로 들어갑니다.
More than half of the budget goes to labor costs.
Formal; 절반 이상 = 'more than half'
nuance: 절반 is Sino-Korean 折半 ('break/fold' 折 + 'half' 半 = literally 'fold something in two'), so it carries the feel of cleanly dividing a whole into two equal portions. Its everyday twin is the one-syllable 반, which is the plain Sino-Korean reading of that same 半: 반 is shorter, more casual, and used constantly (반만 주세요, 반반), whereas the two-character 절반 sounds more deliberate and precise, favored when you're stressing the exactness of the split or writing a report. Note 반 also forms set time expressions (한 시 반 'half past one') and compound words (반값 'half price') where 절반 cannot substitute. Register is neutral; both are fine in polite speech. The English-speaker pitfall is the 'into halves' construction: to say 'cut it in half' you need the goal particle 으로 — 절반으로 자르다 — not a bare noun; learners often drop 으로 and produce the incomplete 절반 잘라요.

mistakes: Saying 절반 잘랐어요 for 'I cut it in half' without the goal particle. Use 절반으로 잘랐어요 — 으로 marks the resulting state.
Using 절반 for a vague 'about half / roughly half'. 절반 is exactly one half; for a rough amount say 반쯤 or 절반쯤.
Swapping 절반 into fixed 반 expressions, e.g. 한 시 절반 for 'half past one'. The set form is 한 시 반.

usage: 일부 directly premodifying a noun, unlike 전부
I paid part of the money.
일부 linked to the whole by 의
examples: 이건 일부만 가져가.
Just take some of this.
Casual; 일부만 = 'only a portion'
회원의 일부가 회의에 반대했어요.
Some of the members opposed the meeting.
일부가 = a subset acting as subject
보도된 내용은 사실의 일부에 불과합니다.
What was reported is only a fraction of the facts.
Formal; 일부에 불과하다 = 'is nothing but a part'
nuance: 일부 is Sino-Korean 一部 ('one' 一 + 'part' 部 = 'one portion'), naming a limited slice of a larger whole. It sits on a spectrum: 일부 (a part) < 절반 (half) < 대부분 (most) < 전부 (all), and its sharpest contrast is with 전부 — 일부 deliberately implies the rest is excluded. Unlike 전부, 일부 CAN stand right before a noun (일부 사람 'some people'), which makes it behave a bit like English 'some'. Distinguish it from 약간: 약간 is about a small degree/amount of something (a little salt), while 일부 is a countable sub-section of a defined whole (some of the members). Register is neutral and slightly bookish; it's everywhere in news and reports. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 일부 to translate 'a few' when you really mean a small number of discrete things — for 'a few people' Koreans more often say 몇몇 사람 or 몇 명; 일부 frames them as 'a faction/portion of the whole' rather than just 'a small number'.

Dropping the 의 that links 일부 to its whole, e.g. 돈 일부를 for 'part of the money' — say 돈의 일부를.

usage: Most of the students are Korean.
Most of the shops are closed.
I use most of my time studying.
examples: 주말엔 대부분 집에서 쉬어.
On weekends I mostly rest at home.
Casual; 대부분 as adverb 'usually/mostly'
참석자의 대부분이 찬성했어요.
Most of the attendees were in favor.
대부분이 marking the majority as subject
설문에 응답한 사람의 대부분이 긍정적으로 평가했습니다.
Most of the survey respondents rated it positively.
Formal report register; 대부분이 with a quantified group
nuance: 대부분 is Sino-Korean 大部分 ('big' 大 + 'part' 部 + 'portion' 分 = 'the large part'), meaning almost all but stopping just short of everything — a small remainder is always implied. On the quantity ladder it sits between 일부 (a portion) and 전부 (the whole), and its key contrast is exactly with 전부: claim 대부분 and you leave a little room, claim 전부 and you leave none. It doubles as an adverb meaning 'mostly/usually' (주말엔 대부분 쉬어요), which 전부 cannot do. Compare 거의 다 ('almost all'), which is a near-synonym but feels more spoken and approximate, while 대부분 is comfortable in both speech and formal writing. As a noun it links to its whole with 의 (학생의 대부분) or premodifies with 대부분의 (대부분의 학생). The English-speaker pitfall is omitting 의 and writing 대부분 학생 by analogy with 'most students' — the natural patterns are 대부분의 학생 or 학생의 대부분.

Saying 대부분 학생 for 'most students' without 의. Use 대부분의 학생 (premodifier) or 학생의 대부분 (noun + of).
Forgetting that adverbial 대부분 means 'usually/mostly', and overusing it for countable nouns where 대부분의 + noun reads better.

usage: 약간 as a degree adverb before an adjective
약간 = a small amount of an uncountable thing
약간의 + noun, the bookish noun use
약간 softening the strength of the state
examples: 국이 약간 짜.
The soup is a bit salty.
Casual; 약간 dialing a quality down a notch
커피에 설탕을 약간만 넣어 주세요.
Please add just a little sugar to my coffee.
약간만 = 'only a little', polite request
이번 분기 매출은 약간 증가했습니다.
Sales rose slightly this quarter.
Formal; 약간 = 'slightly' with a change verb
nuance: 약간 is Sino-Korean 若干 (here meaning 'some small amount / a few'), used both as a degree adverb ('a little, slightly') and, with 의, as a noun ('a small quantity of'). Its closest rivals are 조금 and 좀: 조금 is the everyday native word for 'a little' and is interchangeable in many spots, while 좀 is the contracted, very colloquial form that also functions as a softener in requests (좀 도와주세요). 약간 sounds a shade more measured and is the default when describing a slight degree of a quality (약간 맵다, 약간 다르다) or a small change in formal/written contexts (약간 증가하다). Note it covers small DEGREE and small AMOUNT, unlike 일부, which is a sub-portion of a countable whole. The English-speaker pitfall is putting 약간 after the verb or treating it like a quantity noun on its own: it normally comes right before the adjective/verb it scales (약간 추워요), and when it modifies a noun you need 약간의 (약간의 돈), not a bare 약간 돈.

Writing 약간 돈 for 'a little money'. To modify a noun use 약간의 돈, or rephrase as 돈을 약간 (with a verb).
Confusing it with 일부: 약간 맵다 ('slightly spicy', degree) is fine, but for 'some of the members' you need 일부, not 약간.

usage: 여러 must sit directly before the noun
여러 stressing variety, not just number
examples: 친구 여러 명이 놀러 왔어.
Several friends came over.
Casual; 여러 명 = 'several people' with a counter
여러 문제가 한꺼번에 생겼어요.
Several problems came up at once.
여러 + plural noun as subject
이 사안은 여러 부서가 함께 논의해야 합니다.
This matter must be discussed jointly by several departments.
Formal; 여러 emphasizing multiple distinct parties
nuance: 여러 is a native determiner (관형사) meaning 'several / various / a number of', and its defining trait is that it ONLY ever stands in front of a noun — it can never be a subject, object, or stand alone, and it never takes a particle (no 여러가, no 여러를). Its nearest neighbors are 몇 and 여러 가지: 몇 means 'a few / how many' and asks or implies a small uncertain count (몇 명?), while 여러 asserts 'quite a few, more than two or three' and often adds a flavor of 'various, of different sorts'. For countable people/things you pair it with a counter (여러 명, 여러 번, 여러 개); for 'various kinds' you say 여러 가지. Register is neutral. The big English-speaker pitfall is trying to use 여러 the way you'd use the noun 'several' in 'several came' — Korean cannot say 여러가 왔어요; you must supply a noun, e.g. 여러 사람이 왔어요 or 여러 명이 왔어요.

mistakes: Using 여러 alone as a subject/object, e.g. 여러가 왔어요. 여러 must modify a noun: 여러 사람이 왔어요.
Attaching a particle to 여러 (여러를, 여러가). It's a determiner and takes none; particles go on the noun after it.
Confusing 여러 with 몇: 여러 번 = 'several (many) times' asserts a fair number, while 몇 번 = 'a few / how many times' is small or questioning.

usage: 수량 as subject in a stock context
수량 = the counted number of items
수량 stated with a number + counter
수량 paired with 많다, not 크다
examples: 이거 수량 좀 세 줘.
Count the quantity of these for me.
Casual; 수량 = how many pieces
재고 수량이 부족해서 주문할 수 없어요.
We can't order because the stock quantity is low.
재고 수량 = 'stock quantity', everyday store talk
주문 수량을 정확히 기재해 주시기 바랍니다.
Please state the order quantity accurately.
Formal; 주문 수량 = 'order quantity' on a form
nuance: 수량 is Sino-Korean 數量 ('number' 數 + 'amount' 量 = 'numbered amount'), and it specifically means a COUNTABLE number of discrete items — it lives in shopping, ordering, inventory, and shipping contexts. Compare 양 (量) alone, which means 'amount' in a broader, often uncountable sense (물의 양 'the amount of water', 일의 양 'the amount of work'); you would not say 물의 수량. Compare also 개수 (個數), which narrowly means 'the number of pieces' and is even more strictly about a count, while 수량 can feel a touch more formal/commercial. Because 수량 is about number, it pairs with 많다/적다 ('many/few'), not 크다/작다 ('big/small'). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping the English 'amount' (which English uses for both countable and uncountable) onto 수량 across the board — for liquids, time, work, or emotion you need 양, and for water specifically 물의 수량 sounds wrong; say 물의 양.

Pairing 수량 with 크다/작다. Since it's a count, use 수량이 많다/적다 ('the quantity is large/small').
Confusing 수량 with 수: bare 수 means 'number' abstractly (학생 수 'number of students'), while 수량 implies a counted stock or order amount.

usage: 단위 as subject = unit of measure
It's sold in units of a thousand won.
examples: 길이 단위는 미터야.
The unit of length is the meter.
Casual; 단위 naming a standard measure
이 약은 한 알 단위로 처방돼요.
This medicine is prescribed by the pill.
단위로 = 'by the unit of', one pill at a time
보고서의 금액은 백만 원 단위로 표기되어 있습니다.
The figures in the report are shown in units of one million won.
Formal; 백만 원 단위 = 'million-won units'
nuance: 단위 is Sino-Korean 單位 ('single' 單 + 'position/rank' 位 = 'a single standard place'), meaning a unit of measurement (meter, kilogram, won) and, by extension, the basic block by which something is counted or grouped (가족 단위 'by household', 학년 단위 'by grade'). Its crucial contrast is with 수량: 단위 is the YARDSTICK (kg, m), while 수량 is the COUNT you get when you measure (열 개, 5킬로그램). Don't confuse it either with 단계 ('stage/step', 段階), which sounds similar but means a phase in a process. A very productive pattern is 단위로 ('in/by units of') — 천 원 단위로, 시간 단위로 ('by the hour'). Register is neutral to formal. The English-speaker pitfall is using 단위 for the counted amount itself: English 'a unit of three' tempts learners to say 단위 for the quantity, but the number is 수량/개수 and 단위 only names the measuring standard or grouping.

Dropping the 로 in the 'by units of' pattern, e.g. 천 원 단위 팔아요 — say 천 원 단위로 팔아요.

usage: 두께 with 얇다, the matched adjective
examples: 이 이불 두께 좀 봐, 엄청 두꺼워.
Look how thick this blanket is.

이 유리는 두께가 5밀리미터로 제작되었습니다.

Formal; 두께 with a precise measurement
nuance: 두께 is a native noun built from the adjective 두껍다 ('thick') plus the nominalizing suffix -이/-께, and it names the front-to-back dimension of a flat or layered object — paper, a wall, fabric, glass, a steak. Keep 두께 separate from the other -이 measurement nouns: 길이 (length), 높이 (height), 넓이 (area), 깊이 (depth). Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'thick' covers both flat things and round things, so learners over-apply 두께/두껍다 to ropes, wires, and noodles, where Koreans switch to 굵기/굵다.

usage: 무게 with 무겁다, its matched adjective
examples: 이 가방 무게 장난 아니다.
This bag's weight is no joke.
Casual; 무게 + 무겁다 implied for something heavy
짐 무게가 기준을 넘어서 추가 요금을 냈어요.
The luggage weight exceeded the limit, so I paid an extra fee.
Real situation; 무게 at an airport check-in
택배는 무게에 따라 요금이 달라집니다.
Parcel fees vary according to weight.
Formal; 무게에 따라 = 'depending on weight'
nuance: 무게 is a native noun from the adjective 무겁다 ('heavy') plus the -에/-게 nominalizer, meaning how heavy something is. Its matched adjectives are 무겁다 ('heavy') and 가볍다 ('light'), and the standard verb for measuring it is 재다 (무게를 재다 'to weigh'). Beyond the physical sense, 무게 also carries the figurative meaning of 'gravity, importance, dignity' — 말의 무게 'the weight of one's words', 무게를 잡다 'to put on a serious air'. Keep it distinct from 수량 (how MANY) and from 양 (how much in a general/uncountable sense): a box's 무게 is its heaviness, its 수량 is how many boxes there are. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice: English 'weigh' is one word, but Korean splits it — 무게를 재다 means 'to measure the weight (of something)', whereas the intransitive 'it weighs 5 kg' is 5킬로그램이 나가다 (무게가 나가다), so learners wrongly say 무게를 재다 when they mean 'it weighs ~'.

usage: 길이 with 길다, its matched adjective
examples: 이 끈 길이가 딱 좋아.
This string's length is just right.
Casual; 길이 with 좋다 for a fitting length
머리 길이를 어깨까지 잘랐어요.
I cut my hair length to the shoulders.
Everyday; 길이 in a haircut context
이 다리의 길이는 약 1.2킬로미터에 이릅니다.
The length of this bridge reaches about 1.2 kilometers.
Formal; 길이 with a large measured figure
nuance: 길이 is a native noun from the adjective 길다 ('long') plus the -이 nominalizer, naming the end-to-end (usually horizontal) extent of something. Its matched adjectives are 길다 ('long') and 짧다 ('short'), and you measure it with 재다 (길이를 재다). It belongs to a tidy family of -이 measurement nouns you should keep straight: 길이 (length, side to side), 높이 (height, bottom to top), 깊이 (depth, surface to bottom), 넓이 (area), and the odd one out 두께/굵기 for thickness. The sharp contrast is 길이 vs 높이: a desk's 길이 is how long it is across, its 높이 is how tall it stands — confuse them and a Korean will picture the wrong dimension. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is using 길이 for vertical 'how tall', because English loosely says 'the length of the pole' even when standing upright; in Korean a standing object's vertical measure is 높이, and 길이 implies the laid-flat, lengthwise dimension.

usage: 높이 with 높다, its matched adjective
examples: 이 선반 높이 좀 낮춰 줘.
Lower this shelf's height a bit.
Casual; 높이 with 낮추다 to adjust it
책상 높이를 내 키에 맞게 조절했어요.
I adjusted the desk height to fit my build.
Everyday; 높이 조절 for furniture
이 빌딩의 높이는 123층, 555미터에 달합니다.
This building's height reaches 123 floors and 555 meters.
Formal; 높이 with an impressive figure
nuance: 높이 is a native noun from the adjective 높다 ('high/tall') plus the -이 nominalizer, naming the bottom-to-top (vertical) extent of something — a building, a mountain, a shelf, a jump. A key distinction: for a PERSON's height you don't use 높이 — you use 키 (키가 크다 'is tall'), so 사람의 높이 is wrong and 키 is required. Within the -이 measurement family, the constant trap is 높이 vs 길이: 높이 is how tall something stands upright, 길이 is how long it is laid out lengthwise. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: don't apply 높이 to people (that's 키), and don't pair it with 크다/작다 — even though English says 'big height', Korean says 높이가 높다/낮다. English 'high/tall' collapsing into one word is exactly what trips learners between 키, 높이, and (for length) 길이.
